zones.name: North West
zones.intro: Seven states across the high plains of Hausaland, from the old walled cities of Kano, Katsina and Zaria to Sokoto, seat of the 19th-century caliphate. Sudan savanna gives way to Sahel at the northern border.

zones.name: North East
zones.intro: Six states and the country's widest horizons: the Lake Chad basin, the Gongola valley and the Mambilla Plateau, where Chappal Waddi, Nigeria's highest peak, stands on the Cameroon border.

zones.name: North Central
zones.intro: The Middle Belt: six states and the Federal Capital Territory. The Niger and the Benue meet here at Lokoja, the Jos Plateau rises above the plains, and more languages are spoken than anywhere else in the country.

zones.name: South West
zones.intro: Six states from the Atlantic lagoons to the forest hills of Ekiti, home to old Yoruba cities such as Ile-Ife, Ibadan and Abeokuta, and to Lagos, the largest city in the country.

zones.name: South East
zones.intro: The five smallest and most closely settled states, set between the Niger and the Cross River: plateau, scarp and palm belt, with market cities such as Onitsha and Aba.

zones.name: South South
zones.intro: Six states around the Niger Delta and the Cross River basin: mangrove creeks, the old city of Benin, the port of Calabar and the country's largest remaining rainforest.

states.name: Abia
states.createdNote: Carved out of Imo State on 27 August 1991.

population.source: National Population Commission / National Bureau of Statistics projection

states.terrain: Low, level plains in the south around Aba and Ukwa, rising northwards to rolling hill country around Umuahia, Bende, Ohafia and Arochukwu. The Imo River marks the western border.
states.climate: Humid and tropical. A long rainy season runs from about March to October, heaviest in the south, with a short dry season and harmattan around the turn of the year.
states.vegetation: Lowland rainforest, now mostly farmland and oil-palm bush, with freshwater swamp forest in the far south.
highlands: Hill country of Ohafia, Bende and Arochukwu
peoples: Igbo, in many distinct communities with their own dialects and customs, among them Ngwa, Umuahia (Ohuhu and Ibeku), Ohafia, Abiriba, Aro, Bende, Isuikwuato and Ukwa
Residents from every part of Nigeria in Aba, one of the country's great trading and manufacturing cities

spotlight.title: Akwete cloth
spotlight.kicker: Woven by the women of Akwete, in Ukwa East
spotlight.description: Akwete is a town and a cloth. Its women weave on a wide upright loom, far broader than the narrow strip looms used elsewhere in West Africa, so that a wrapper comes off the loom as a single panel. Motifs are worked into the ground weave in a second, raised thread, and many have names, such as ikaki, the tortoise, once kept for royalty. Weavers guard their own patterns and are said to receive new ones in dreams. The craft passes from mother to daughter, and a fine Akwete wrapper is still given at weddings and worn for ceremonies.

foods.name: Ofe achara
foods.description: A soup of tender achara shoots with moulded balls of ground melon seed (akpụrụakpụ egusi), cooked with stockfish, meat and ụkazị leaf. One of the best-known dishes of Abia State.

foods.name: Ofe ụkazị
foods.description: A thick soup of finely sliced ụkazị leaves with palm oil, meat and dried fish, eaten with fufu or garri.

foods.name: Ụkwa
foods.description: African breadfruit seeds cooked soft into a pottage, or roasted and eaten with coconut or palm kernel.

crafts: Akwete weaving, on the wide upright loom.
Made in Aba: thousands of small workshops around Ariaria market cut and stitch shoes, bags, belts and clothing that sell across West Africa.
Blacksmithing, for which the smiths of Abiriba were long known.
The Ohafia war dance, ikpirikpi ọgụ: its costume includes a carved board hung with symbolic heads, carried on the lead dancer's head.
states.attire: Men wear a wrapper or trousers with a tunic, often the lion-patterned isiagu, and a cap; titled men wear red caps. Women wear a blouse with two wrappers and a head tie, with beads for occasions, and Akwete cloth for the grandest. Ohafia men have a distinct war-dance dress. This is Igbo dress in many local forms, not one uniform.

places.name: National War Museum, Umuahia
places.description: Aircraft, armoured vehicles, ships and locally made weapons of the civil war, with the bunker of the wartime Voice of Biafra radio.

places.name: Arochukwu
places.description: The old Aro capital, with the cave and gorge of the Ibini Ukpabi oracle, called the Long Juju by the British.

places.name: Azumini Blue River
places.description: A clear, blue-tinted river with sandy banks in the south of the state.

places.name: Ariaria International Market, Aba
places.description: A vast market and workshop district, the home of Aba's shoe and garment makers.

places.name: Akwete
places.description: The weaving town, where cloth can be bought from the women who make it.

places.name: National Museum of Colonial History, Aba
places.description: Photographs and documents of the colonial period and the road to independence.

history.event: The Aro, from their capital at Arochukwu, build a network of trade and settlement across the region, backed by the authority of the Ibini Ukpabi oracle.
A British military expedition defeats the Aro and destroys the oracle's shrine.
The Women's War begins at Oloko, near Umuahia, when women rise against the threat of taxation and the conduct of warrant chiefs. It spreads to Aba and far beyond, and forces changes in colonial rule.
Umuahia is the capital of Biafra after the fall of Enugu, until federal forces take the town in April 1969.
Abia State is created on 27 August from Imo State.
The Afikpo area is transferred to the new Ebonyi State.

notableFigures.name: Alvan Ikoku (1900–1971)
notableFigures.note: Educator from Arochukwu, founder of one of the first African-owned secondary schools in Nigeria.

notableFigures.name: Michael Okpara (1920–1984)
notableFigures.note: Physician from the Umuahia area. Premier of the Eastern Region from 1959 to 1966.

notableFigures.name: J. T. U. Aguiyi-Ironsi (1924–1966)
notableFigures.note: Soldier from Umuahia. Nigeria's first military Head of State, in 1966.

notableFigures.name: Nwankwo Kanu (born 1976)
notableFigures.note: Footballer, born in Owerri to a family from Arochukwu. Olympic gold medallist in 1996.

didYouKnow: The name Abia is said to be made from the initials of four of its old divisions, beginning with Aba, Bende and Isuikwuato. Sources differ on whether the fourth is Arochukwu or Afikpo.
The 1929 Women's War, often called the Aba Women's Riot, was one of the largest protests against colonial rule in West Africa.
Umuahia was the capital of Biafra for about a year and a half.
"Aba-made" was once a put-down for local goods. The city's makers now wear it as a trademark.

states.name: Adamawa
states.createdNote: Created on 27 August 1991, when Gongola State was divided into Adamawa and Taraba.

population.source: National Population Commission / National Bureau of Statistics projection

states.terrain: A land of valleys and mountains. The Benue crosses the state from the Cameroon border, joined by the Gongola near Numan. Mountain ranges stand along the eastern frontier: the Mandara in the north, the Atlantika in the south-east and the Shebshi in the south-west, where Mount Dimlang rises to about 2,040 metres.
states.climate: Tropical, with a wet season from about April to October and a dry season from November to March. The north is hotter and drier than the south; the highlands are cooler.
states.vegetation: Sudan savanna in the north, Guinea savanna woodland in the south, and grassland and forest patches on the mountains.
peoples: Bwatiye (Bachama) and Bata, along the Benue
Kilba, Marghi and Kamwe (Higi), in the north
Mbula, Lunguda, Yungur, Verre, Gude and Sukur, among many others
Hausa and other communities in the towns
languages: Fulfulde, the common language of the state
More than 50 other languages; over 100 ethnic groups are counted

spotlight.title: Sukur
spotlight.kicker: Nigeria's first World Heritage Site
spotlight.description: Sukur sits on a plateau in the Mandara Mountains, above the plains of Madagali. A stone-paved way climbs to the palace of the Hidi, its chief, a ring of dry-stone walls and granaries looking out over terraced fields that have been farmed for centuries. Below it are the villages, with their sunken animal pens, threshing floors, shrines and the remains of the furnaces in which Sukur's smiths smelted iron for trade across the region. UNESCO listed the Sukur Cultural Landscape in 1999 as a remarkably intact record of a society and its land.

foods.name: Marghi special
foods.description: A tamarind-sharp soup of fresh fish with sorrel and other greens. A dish of the Marghi people of the north-east.

foods.name: Tuwo and leaf soups
foods.description: Maize or guinea-corn swallow with soups of baobab leaf, sorrel or okra.

foods.name: Kindirmo and nono
foods.description: Yoghurt and fermented milk from Fulani herds, taken with fura or on their own.

foods.name: Benue fish
foods.description: Fresh and smoked fish from the river, a speciality of Numan and Yola.

crafts: Decorated calabashes: Fulani women carve and burn fine patterns into gourds used for milk.
Ironworking, an old speciality of Sukur and the Mandara hills.
Pottery and weaving among the peoples of the Benue valley.
states.attire: Fulani men wear flowing gowns and embroidered caps, and women wrappers and beads. The Bwatiye, Chamba, Kilba and other peoples each have their own festival dress.

places.name: Sukur Cultural Landscape
places.description: The hilltop palace, terraces and villages above Madagali.

places.name: Lamido's Palace, Yola
places.description: Seat of the Lamido of Adamawa, with a palace museum.

places.name: Three Sisters Rock, Song
places.description: Three tall rock pillars standing side by side.

places.name: Kamale Peak, Michika
places.description: A sharp rock spire in the Mandara Mountains.

places.name: Ruwan Zafi, Lamurde
places.description: A hot spring.

places.name: Kiri Dam
places.description: A reservoir on the Gongola River.

history.event: Modibbo Adama receives a flag from Usman dan Fodio and founds the emirate of Fombina, later called Adamawa after him.
Yola is founded as the emirate's capital.
The British take Yola. The emirate's lands are divided between British Nigeria and German Kamerun.
In a United Nations plebiscite, the Northern Cameroons vote to join Nigeria. The area includes Mubi, Michika and Ganye.
Gongola State is created.
Adamawa State is created on 27 August.
Sukur is inscribed as a World Heritage Site.
Insurgents seize Mubi and other northern towns. They are driven out over the following months, and people begin to return.

notableFigures.name: Modibbo Adama (died c. 1847)
notableFigures.note: Scholar and founder of the emirate that bears his name.

notableFigures.name: Bamanga Tukur (born 1935)
notableFigures.note: Businessman and politician. Governor of the old Gongola State.

notableFigures.name: Murtala Nyako (born 1942)
notableFigures.note: Naval officer from Mayo-Belwa. Governor of Adamawa from 2007 to 2014.

notableFigures.name: Atiku Abubakar (born 1946)
notableFigures.note: From Jada. Vice-President of Nigeria from 1999 to 2007.

didYouKnow: The state is named after Modibbo Adama.
Sukur, listed in 1999, was the first World Heritage Site in Nigeria.
More than 100 ethnic groups live in the state.
Part of the state was once German and later British-administered Cameroon, and joined Nigeria by vote in 1961.

states.name: Akwa Ibom
states.createdNote: Carved out of Cross River State on 23 September 1987.

population.source: National Population Commission / National Bureau of Statistics projection

states.terrain: A coastal plain between two estuaries, the Imo River in the west and the Cross River in the east, with the Qua Iboe River running through the middle to the sea at Ibeno. The shore is a mix of long sand beaches and mangrove-lined creeks and river mouths. Inland the ground is a low, gently rolling plain of sandy soils, cut by steep ravines in places.
states.climate: Hot, humid and very wet. Rain falls in most months, heaviest from about April to October, with a short drier spell around the turn of the year.
states.vegetation: Mangrove along the tidal creeks and estuaries, with freshwater swamp forest behind it. Inland the rainforest has largely given way to farmland and dense stands of oil palm and raffia palm.
peoples: Ibibio, the largest group, across the centre of the state
Annang, in the west around Ikot Ekpene and Abak
Oron (Oro), on the Cross River estuary
languages: About 20 languages are spoken as first languages in the state

spotlight.title: The raffia work of Ikot Ekpene
spotlight.kicker: Why they call it the Raffia City
spotlight.description: Ikot Ekpene is the cultural capital of the Annang people, in country where the raffia palm grows thick along the streams. Its craftspeople turn raffia fibre into cloth and work it into bags, hats, mats, shoes and furniture. The trade has given the town its nickname and a long line of roadside workshops. Alongside the weavers work wood carvers, heirs to the tradition that produced the masks and figures of the Annang and Ibibio now held in museums around the world.

foods.name: Afang soup
foods.description: Finely shredded afang leaves and waterleaf cooked down with palm oil, beef, stockfish, periwinkle and crayfish. Shared with neighbouring Cross River, and the dish most visitors ask for first.

foods.name: Edikang ikong
foods.description: A dense, dark-green soup of fluted pumpkin leaves and waterleaf with assorted meats and seafood.

foods.name: Afere atama
foods.description: A soup of palm fruit extract scented with atama leaves, cooked with fresh and smoked fish, periwinkle and meat.

foods.name: Ekpang nkukwo
foods.description: Grated cocoyam and water yam wrapped in tender cocoyam leaves and simmered with periwinkle, fish and palm oil.

crafts: Raffia weaving and plaiting at Ikot Ekpene.
Wood carving: the masks and figures of Annang and Ibibio carvers, and the carved ancestor figures of Oron, are among the best-known sculpture of south-eastern Nigeria.
Raffia and cane furniture.
states.attire: For occasions, men commonly wear a wrapper with a long shirt, a hat and a walking stick, and women a blouse with wrappers or a long gown, with beads. Each of the state's peoples has its own names, cloths and customs of dress.

places.name: Ibeno Beach
places.description: A very long stretch of sand on the Atlantic, beside the mouth of the Qua Iboe River.

places.name: Oron Museum
places.description: A national museum on the Cross River estuary, known for its collection of carved wooden ancestor figures.

places.name: Ikot Abasi
places.description: An old river port with colonial-era buildings and a memorial to the women killed in the Women's War of 1929.

places.name: Ikot Ekpene raffia market
places.description: Workshops and stalls of raffia goods and carvings along the town's main road.

places.name: Godswill Akpabio International Stadium, Uyo
places.description: A modern stadium that hosts the national football team.

history.event: The Qua Iboe Mission begins work at Ibeno.
The Ibibio Union is formed. It becomes one of the most influential ethnic unions in colonial Nigeria and later sends students abroad on scholarships.
The Women's War spreads across the area. In December, colonial troops shoot dead protesting women at the port then called Opobo, now Ikot Abasi.
Akwa Ibom State is created on 23 September from Cross River State, with Uyo as capital.
Ibom Air, owned by the state government, begins flying.

notableFigures.name: Udo Udoma (1917–1998)
notableFigures.note: Jurist from Ikot Abasi. Chief Justice of Uganda and a justice of the Supreme Court of Nigeria.

notableFigures.name: Clement Isong (1920–2000)
notableFigures.note: Economist from Eket. Governor of the Central Bank of Nigeria and later of the old Cross River State.

notableFigures.name: Dominic Ekandem (1917–1995)
notableFigures.note: Born at Obio Ibiono. In 1976 he became the first Nigerian cardinal.

notableFigures.name: Victor Attah (born 1938)
notableFigures.note: Architect. Governor of Akwa Ibom State from 1999 to 2007.

notableFigures.name: Vincent Enyeama (born 1982)
notableFigures.note: Goalkeeper and former captain of the national football team.

didYouKnow: The state is named after the Qua Iboe River.
With 31 local government areas, Akwa Ibom has more than any other state in the South South.
About 20 languages are spoken as first languages in the state.
Much of Nigeria's offshore oil is produced in waters off its coast.

states.name: Anambra
states.createdNote: The present state dates from 27 August 1991, when the old Anambra State of 1976 was divided into Anambra and Enugu.

population.source: National Population Commission / National Bureau of Statistics projection

states.terrain: Two landscapes. In the west and north, the broad floodplains of the Niger and the Anambra River. In the east and south, a low sandstone upland around Awka, Agulu and Nnewi, deeply cut in places by erosion gullies.
states.climate: Tropical, with rain from about April to October and a dry season with harmattan from November to February. The river plains flood late in the rains.
states.vegetation: Rainforest long since turned to farmland, oil palm and settlement, with grassy floodplain along the rivers and savanna woodland in the north.
peoples: Igbo, in many towns and clans with their own dialects, from the riverine Anam and Ogbaru to Onitsha, Awka, Nnewi and Aguata
Igala-speaking communities on the northern river border
Traders and residents from across Nigeria and West Africa in Onitsha

spotlight.title: The Ofala of Onitsha
spotlight.kicker: Every October
spotlight.description: Once a year the Obi of Onitsha comes out before his people. The Ofala closes a week-long retreat in which the king withdraws from public view, and it is tied to the new yam season. On the day, a cannon shot announces him. The red-capped chiefs, the ndichie, arrive with their own followers and pay homage in order of seniority, and the Obi appears in ceremonial robes and dances in the palace square, a sight seen at no other time. Age grades, women's groups and visiting rulers follow. Other towns in the state hold their own Ofala, each for its own king.

foods.name: Ofe ọnụgbụ
foods.description: Bitterleaf soup. The leaves are washed until only a trace of bitterness is left, then cooked with cocoyam paste, palm oil, ogiri, stockfish and meat.

foods.name: Ofe nsala
foods.description: "White soup": a light, peppery broth made without palm oil, thickened with pounded yam and usually cooked with fresh catfish. A dish of the river towns.

foods.name: Abacha
foods.description: Shredded dried cassava dressed with palm oil, ụgba (fermented oil bean), garden egg and fish. Offered to guests and sold at every market.

foods.name: Akpụ
foods.description: Fermented cassava fufu, the usual swallow with both soups.

crafts: Bronze casting: the bronzes of Igbo-Ukwu, made in the 9th century, are among the oldest and most intricate castings known from West Africa.
Blacksmithing: the smiths of Awka travelled and settled across the region for centuries, making tools, ritual staffs and guns.
Wood carving: Awka carvers are known for panelled doors, stools and title-holders' regalia.
Uli: the women's art of drawing on skin and walls, practised in the villages of the state.
states.attire: Men wear a wrapper or trousers with a tunic, often the lion-patterned isiagu, and a cap; ọzọ title holders wear red caps, sometimes with an eagle feather, and carry a staff. Women wear a blouse with two wrappers and a head tie, with coral or other beads. Local custom varies from town to town.

places.name: Ogbunike Caves
places.description: A network of sandstone caves in a forested valley, reached by a long flight of steps and visited for centuries as a sacred place.

places.name: Igbo-Ukwu
places.description: The town where the 9th-century bronzes were found, with a small museum. The finest pieces are in the National Museum, Lagos.

places.name: Agulu Lake
places.description: A quiet lake below the upland, home to crocodiles that local custom protects.

places.name: Onitsha Main Market and the Niger Bridge
places.description: One of the largest markets in West Africa, beside the 1965 bridge that carries the main road east across the Niger.

places.name: Nri
places.description: Seat of an ancient priestly kingship, with a museum of Igbo civilisation.

places.name: Ogba Ukwu, Owerre-Ezukala
places.description: A large cave and waterfall in the south-east of the state.

history.event: Craftsmen at Igbo-Ukwu cast elaborate bronze vessels and ornaments and bury them with a person of high rank.
The kingdom of Nri is established; some traditions place it earlier. Its priest-kings hold ritual, not military, authority over much of Igboland.
A trading post and a Church Missionary Society station are opened at Onitsha.
A man digging a cistern at Igbo-Ukwu uncovers the first bronzes. Excavations follow from 1959.
The Niger Bridge opens between Onitsha and Asaba.
Anambra State is created, with its capital at Enugu.
Enugu State is separated, and Awka becomes capital of the present Anambra State.

notableFigures.name: Nnamdi Azikiwe (1904–1996)
notableFigures.note: Journalist and statesman of an Onitsha family, born in Zungeru. First President of Nigeria.

notableFigures.name: Kenneth Dike (1917–1983)
notableFigures.note: Historian from Awka, a founder of modern African historical scholarship.

notableFigures.name: Chinua Achebe (1930–2013)
notableFigures.note: Novelist from Ogidi, author of Things Fall Apart.

notableFigures.name: Chukwuemeka Odumegwu Ojukwu (1933–2011)
notableFigures.note: Soldier and politician of a Nnewi family, born in Zungeru. Leader of Biafra.

notableFigures.name: Emeka Anyaoku (born 1933)
notableFigures.note: Diplomat from Obosi. Commonwealth Secretary-General from 1990 to 2000.

didYouKnow: The name is an English rendering of Omambala, the Igbo name of the Anambra River.
After Lagos, Anambra is the smallest state by area, and one of the most densely settled.
From the 1940s to the 1960s, Onitsha's printers turned out thousands of cheap pamphlets of stories, plays and advice, now studied as Onitsha Market Literature.
Nnewi is a centre of motor-parts trade and manufacturing, and home to the first Nigerian-owned vehicle assembly plant.
The Ogbunike Caves are on Nigeria's Tentative List for UNESCO World Heritage.

states.name: Bauchi
states.createdNote: Created on 3 February 1976. Gombe was carved out of it in 1996.

population.source: National Population Commission / National Bureau of Statistics projection

states.terrain: The state runs from the edge of the Jos Plateau in the south-west, where the land is high and hilly, down to flat, dry plains in the north. Between them lie the wooded valleys of the Gongola and its tributaries, including the Gaji, which flows through Yankari.
states.climate: Hot, with rain from about May to September. The south gets about 1,300 mm a year and the north about 700 mm.
states.vegetation: Sudan savanna in the south and centre, with wooded river valleys, thinning to Sahel savanna in the north.
highlands: Bauchi Plateau, the eastern edge of the Jos Plateau
peoples: Around 55 groups are counted in the state
languages: Many Chadic languages, among them Gera, Zaar, Bole and Warji

spotlight.title: Yankari and the Wikki warm spring
spotlight.kicker: The best-known wildlife reserve in Nigeria
spotlight.description: Yankari is a great tract of savanna woodland along the Gaji River, protected since the 1950s. It holds the largest surviving population of elephants in Nigeria, with buffalo, hippopotamus, roan antelope, waterbuck, baboons and a few remaining lions. At its centre is Wikki, a spring that pours from under a sandstone cliff into a clear pool at a constant 31 °C, all year. People have lived here for a long time: the reserve also contains old iron-smelting furnaces, dwelling caves cut into the sandstone and 139 wells dug to store water.

foods.name: Masa
foods.description: Small, tender cakes of fermented rice batter fried in a pitted clay or iron pan. Bauchi's are the most famous in the north, eaten with pumpkin stew, pepper or honey.

foods.name: Miyar taushe
foods.description: A stew of pumpkin, groundnut and greens, the usual partner for masa and tuwo.

foods.name: Tuwon masara
foods.description: A firm swallow of maize flour, eaten with baobab-leaf or okra soup.

foods.name: Kunun gyaɗa
foods.description: A smooth gruel of rice and groundnut milk.

crafts: Pottery, weaving and blacksmithing in the towns and villages.
Leatherwork and embroidered caps and gowns.
states.attire: Hausa and Fulani men wear the babban riga with an embroidered cap, and women a wrapper, blouse and veil. The many other peoples of the state have their own festival dress.

places.name: Yankari Game Reserve
places.description: Savanna, elephants and the Wikki warm spring.

places.name: Tomb of Abubakar Tafawa Balewa
places.description: The memorial in Bauchi to Nigeria's first Prime Minister.

places.name: Emir's Palace, Bauchi
places.description: Seat of the emirate founded by Yakubu.

places.name: Sumu Wildlife Park
places.description: A park north of Bauchi with giraffe, zebra and antelope.

history.event: Yakubu, a student of Usman dan Fodio, founds the emirate of Bauchi. He is the only flag-bearer of the jihad who was not Fulani.
The British occupy Bauchi.
Yankari is set aside as a game reserve. It opens to visitors in 1962.
Bauchi State is created on 3 February.
Gombe State is carved out.

notableFigures.name: Yakubu of Bauchi (reigned c. 1805–1845)
notableFigures.note: Founder and first emir of Bauchi.

notableFigures.name: Abubakar Tafawa Balewa (1912–1966)
notableFigures.note: Teacher from the town of Tafawa Balewa. The first and only Prime Minister of Nigeria.

notableFigures.name: Sa'adu Zungur (1915–1958)
notableFigures.note: Poet, teacher and nationalist, one of the first northern voices for political reform.

didYouKnow: The state is said to be named after a hunter called Baushe, who lived here before Yakubu came.
Around 55 ethnic groups live in the state.
Yankari's elephants are the largest surviving herd in Nigeria.
The water of the Wikki spring stays at about 31 °C throughout the year.

states.name: Bayelsa
states.createdNote: Carved out of Rivers State on 1 October 1996.

population.source: National Population Commission / National Bureau of Statistics projection

states.terrain: The heart of the Niger Delta. Near the state's northern tip the Niger divides into the Nun and Forcados rivers, which split again into a web of smaller channels on their way to the sea. Almost the whole state is flat, low-lying land between them. Three belts run parallel to the coast: freshwater swamp forest inland, flooded for months each year; a wide band of mangrove threaded with tidal creeks; and sandy barrier islands on the Atlantic. Many towns stand on river banks or islands and are reached only by boat.
states.climate: Hot, humid and among the wettest parts of Nigeria, with rain in most months and close to 3,000 mm in a year. Rivers rise late in the rains and flood the low ground.
states.vegetation: Mangrove forest in the tidal zone, freshwater swamp forest and raffia swamp inland, and strips of rainforest on higher levees and beach ridges.
peoples: Ijaw (Izon), in many clans, each with its own dialect and territory, among them Kolokuma, Opokuma, Ekpetiama, Bomo and the clans of Southern Ijaw
Nembe and the related people of Brass and Akassa
Isoko and Urhobo communities in the north-west

spotlight.title: The boat regatta
spotlight.kicker: The river on parade
spotlight.description: In a country of water, the great public show is held on it. For festivals, the installation of a king or the visit of an honoured guest, the towns of the Delta bring out their big canoes. Each carries dozens of paddlers in matching dress, striking the water in time to drums and song, with a dancer or a masquerade at the prow and flags flying from poles. The boats recall the war canoes and trading canoes on which the old city-states of Nembe and Brass were built. Crews race, wheel and salute before the crowd on the bank, and the town that puts out the finest boat wins the day.

foods.name: Kekefiyai
foods.description: Chopped unripe plantain cooked into a pottage with palm oil, fresh and dried fish, shrimp and pepper.

foods.name: Fresh fish pepper soup
foods.description: Fish straight from the river in a thin, fiery broth, eaten with boiled yam or plantain.

foods.name: Onunu
foods.description: Boiled yam and ripe plantain pounded together with palm oil, served with fish pepper soup. An Ijaw dish, also made in Rivers State.

crafts: Canoe building: dugout canoes carved from single trunks, from small fishing boats to the large canoes used in regattas.
Fishing gear: nets, traps and baskets woven from raffia and cane.
Masquerade headpieces carved in the form of fish and other water creatures, worn for dances that honour water spirits.
states.attire: Men often wear a long shirt over a wrapper with a hat and a walking stick, and women a blouse with wrappers and a head tie, with coral beads for occasions. Each people has its own names and styles.

places.name: Oloibiri
places.description: The town near which Nigeria's first commercial oil well was drilled in 1956. The capped wellhead is kept as a monument.

places.name: Twon-Brass and Akassa
places.description: Old trading ports on the Atlantic, with long beaches and the remains of 19th-century trading posts.

places.name: Nembe
places.description: Capital of one of the historic city-states of the Delta.

places.name: Ox-bow Lake, Yenagoa
places.description: A curved lake left by an old river channel, with a waterfront in the capital.

history.event: Nembe and Brass prosper as city-states trading with European ships, first in slaves and later in palm oil.
Led by King Koko, the people of Nembe attack the Royal Niger Company's headquarters at Akassa, after the company shuts them out of their trade.
Oil is found in commercial quantity at Oloibiri. The first cargo is exported in 1958.
Isaac Adaka Boro declares a Niger Delta Republic. The rising is put down after twelve days.
Bayelsa State is created on 1 October, with Yenagoa as capital.
Ijaw youths issue the Kaiama Declaration, calling for control of the Delta's resources by its people.

notableFigures.name: Ernest Ikoli (1893–1960)
notableFigures.note: Journalist and nationalist from Nembe, a founder of the Nigerian Youth Movement.

notableFigures.name: Gabriel Okara (1921–2019)
notableFigures.note: Poet and novelist, born at Bomoundi. Author of The Voice.

notableFigures.name: Melford Okilo (1933–2008)
notableFigures.note: Politician from the Ogbia area. First civilian governor of the old Rivers State.

notableFigures.name: Isaac Adaka Boro (1938–1968)
notableFigures.note: Born at Oloibiri. Leader of the 1966 rising and a symbol of the Delta's struggle for a fair share of its wealth.

notableFigures.name: Goodluck Jonathan (born 1957)
notableFigures.note: From Otuoke. Governor of Bayelsa and President of Nigeria from 2010 to 2015.

didYouKnow: The name is made from the initials of three old local government areas: Brass (BALGA), Yenagoa (YELGA) and Sagbama (SALGA).
Bayelsa has eight local government areas, the fewest of any state.
By the 2006 census it had the smallest population of any state.
Nigeria's oil industry began here, at Oloibiri.

states.name: Benue
states.createdNote: Created on 3 February 1976 from Benue-Plateau State. Its Igala-speaking western part went to Kogi in 1991.

population.source: National Population Commission / National Bureau of Statistics projection

states.terrain: Low, gently rolling country in the trough of the Benue, mostly between 100 and 250 metres above sea level, with occasional rocky hills. The river crosses the state from east to west and is joined by its largest tributary, the Katsina-Ala. In the south-east the land rises towards the Cameroon highlands.
states.climate: Tropical savanna, with a wet season from about April to October and a dry season from November to March.
states.vegetation: Guinea savanna woodland and tall grass, with forest in the south and along the rivers. The deep soils of the river plains make this some of the best farmland in the country.
highlands: Hill country of Kwande, towards Cameroon
peoples: Tiv, the largest group, across the east and centre
Etulo, Jukun, Akweya, Nyifon and other smaller peoples
Hausa and Igbo traders and settlers in the towns

spotlight.title: Kwagh-hir
spotlight.kicker: The storytelling theatre of the Tiv
spotlight.description: Kwagh-hir means something magical. It grew out of the Tiv habit of telling stories at night after the day's farm work, and in the 1960s it became a full theatre. A narrator calls up each tale, and it is acted out by carved puppets worked from beneath a platform, and by masquerades of animals and spirits that dance into the arena to music and song. The stories are old fables and sharp comments on current life, side by side. UNESCO added Kwagh-hir to its Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2019.

foods.name: Pounded yam
foods.description: Benue is Nigeria's yam country. Boiled yam is pounded smooth and eaten with soup at almost every table. The Tiv call it ruam kumen.

foods.name: Okoho soup
foods.description: An Idoma soup made slippery with the sap of the okoho vine, cooked with bush meat or fish and eaten with pounded yam.

foods.name: Beniseed soup
foods.description: A rich soup of ground sesame seeds, grown widely in the state.

foods.name: Roasted yam and palm oil
foods.description: Yam roasted over coals and dipped in peppered palm oil. Roadside food along every highway.

crafts: A'nger: the black-and-white striped cloth of the Tiv, woven in narrow bands and worn for every important occasion.
The red-and-black striped cloth of the Idoma.
Carved puppets, masks and stools.
Pottery.
states.attire: The Tiv wear a'nger, black and white stripes, as wrappers, gowns, caps and sashes. The Idoma wear red and black stripes, colours adopted in the 1980s. The Igede wear blue, black and white. Each is at once everyday pride and ceremonial dress.

places.name: The Benue at Makurdi
places.description: The wide river, its two bridges and its sandbanks and beaches in the dry season.

places.name: Ikwe Wildlife Park
places.description: A small park and resort near Igbor.

places.name: Enemabia Warm Spring
places.description: A warm spring.

places.name: Ushongo hills
places.description: Rocky hills in the Tiv country.

places.name: Tor Tiv's Palace, Gboko
places.description: Seat of the paramount ruler of the Tiv.

history.event: The office of Tor Tiv, a single paramount ruler for the Tiv, is created.
Uprisings in the Tiv country against the regional government.
Benue-Plateau State is created.
Benue State is created on 3 February, with Makurdi as capital.
The Igala and Bassa areas become part of the new Kogi State.
Clashes between farmers and herders have cost many lives and driven farming families from their land.

notableFigures.name: Joseph Tarka (1932–1980)
notableFigures.note: Tiv politician and leader of the United Middle Belt Congress, who campaigned for a Middle Belt region.

notableFigures.name: Aper Aku (1938–1988)
notableFigures.note: First civilian governor of Benue State.

notableFigures.name: David Mark (born 1948)
notableFigures.note: Soldier and politician from Otukpo. President of the Senate from 2007 to 2015.

notableFigures.name: 2Baba (born 1975)
notableFigures.note: Singer Innocent Idibia, of an Idoma family. One of the makers of modern Nigerian pop.

didYouKnow: The state is named after the River Benue.
Benue is called the Food Basket of the Nation: it is a leading producer of yam, soybean, sesame and citrus.
Of its 23 local government areas, 14 are in the Tiv country, 7 in the Idoma and 2 in the Igede.
It shares a short border with Cameroon.

states.name: Borno
states.createdNote: Created on 3 February 1976. Yobe was carved out of it in 1991.

population.source: National Population Commission / National Bureau of Statistics projection
population.note: The 2006 census counted 4,171,104. Many people have been displaced since 2009, so recent figures are especially uncertain.

states.terrain: Most of the state is the flat plain of the Chad Basin, sloping almost imperceptibly towards Lake Chad in the north-east. The lake is shallow and has shrunk greatly since the 1960s. The south is higher: the volcanic Biu Plateau, and in the south-east the Gwoza Hills, the northern end of the Mandara Mountains.
states.climate: Hot and dry. Rain falls for four to five months, from about June to September, and less in the north. The harmattan blows from December to February.
states.vegetation: Sahel savanna in the north, with thorn scrub and seasonal grassland; Sudan savanna in the centre and south; and woodland on the Biu Plateau.
peoples: Bura and Pabir (Babur), on the Biu Plateau
Marghi and Kibaku (Chibok), in the south
The hill peoples of Gwoza, among them Mafa, Glavda and Dghwede
languages: The Biu–Mandara languages of the south and the hills

spotlight.title: A thousand years of Borno
spotlight.kicker: The heritage of Kanem–Bornu
spotlight.description: Borno is heir to one of the longest-lived states in African history. The Sayfawa kings ruled first Kanem, east of Lake Chad, and then Borno, for the better part of a thousand years. Their empire traded across the Sahara, exchanged embassies with North Africa and was known for its mounted, armoured cavalry and its scholars. In the 19th century the scholar Muhammad al-Kanemi rallied Borno, and his descendants, the Shehus, took the throne. The Shehu of Borno still holds court in Maiduguri, and Kanuri language, dress, horsemanship and learning carry that history forward.

foods.name: Biski
foods.description: Coarsely ground maize or millet, steamed and eaten with stew or soup. A staple grain food of Borno.

foods.name: Miyar kuka with dried fish
foods.description: Baobab-leaf soup cooked with smoked or dried fish from Lake Chad.

foods.name: Fura da nono
foods.description: Spiced millet dough balls crumbled into fermented milk.

foods.name: Kilishi
foods.description: Thin sheets of dried, spiced beef.

crafts: Embroidered caps: the tall, finely stitched cap of Borno is worn across the north.
Leatherwork and horse trappings for the Shehu's cavalry.
Pottery and weaving in the south.
states.attire: Kanuri men wear a long gown with the embroidered Borno cap; titleholders wear a turban. Kanuri women wear wrappers and a veil, with plaited hair and henna. The Shuwa, Bura, Marghi and hill peoples have their own dress.

places.name: Shehu's Palace, Maiduguri
places.description: Seat of the Shehu of Borno.

places.name: Kukawa
places.description: The 19th-century capital, with the tombs of the Shehus.

places.name: Rabih's Fort, Dikwa
places.description: The stronghold of the conqueror Rabih, who ruled Borno in the 1890s.

places.name: Biu Plateau
places.description: Volcanic hills in the cooler south, at around 700 metres above sea level.

places.name: Sanda Kyarimi Park, Maiduguri
places.description: The city's zoo and gardens.

places.name: Lake Alau
places.description: A reservoir near Maiduguri.

history.event: The kingdom of Kanem grows up east of Lake Chad under the Sayfawa dynasty.
Mai Ali Gaji builds a new capital at Ngazargamu.
Ngazargamu is sacked. Muhammad al-Kanemi leads Borno's resistance.
Al-Kanemi founds Kukawa, which becomes the capital.
Rabih conquers Borno and rules from Dikwa until he is killed in 1900.
Maiduguri is established as the capital.
Borno State is created on 3 February.
An insurgency has killed tens of thousands of people in the north-east and displaced many more, most of them in Borno. Maiduguri has sheltered many of them, and rebuilding and resettlement continue.

notableFigures.name: Idris Alooma (reigned c. 1570–1603)
notableFigures.note: The king under whom Borno is often said to have reached its height.

notableFigures.name: Muhammad al-Amin al-Kanemi (1776–1837)
notableFigures.note: Scholar and statesman, founder of the line of the Shehus.

notableFigures.name: Kashim Ibrahim (1910–1990)
notableFigures.note: Teacher and politician. The first Nigerian Governor of the Northern Region.

notableFigures.name: Kashim Shettima (born 1966)
notableFigures.note: Governor of Borno from 2011 to 2019 and Vice-President of Nigeria from 2023.

didYouKnow: Borno is the second-largest state by area, after Niger.
It is the only state that borders three countries: Niger, Chad and Cameroon.
Its slogan is Home of Peace.
The Sayfawa dynasty of Kanem and Borno is counted among the longest-reigning in history.

states.name: Cross River
states.createdNote: Created as South-Eastern State; renamed Cross River State in 1976.

population.source: National Population Commission / National Bureau of Statistics projection

states.terrain: Three landscapes from south to north. Mangrove creeks and the wide Cross River estuary on the coast. The forested Oban Hills in the centre. Then open country rising to the Obudu Plateau on the Cameroon border, which reaches about 1,700 metres above sea level.
states.climate: Humid and tropical. Calabar is among the wettest cities in Nigeria, with more than 3,000 mm of rain a year. The Obudu Plateau is cool enough for mist and cold nights.
states.vegetation: Mangrove on the coast, lowland rainforest across the centre, forest–savanna mosaic in the north and montane grassland on the plateau.
peoples: Many more: this is one of the most linguistically varied states in the country

spotlight.title: Carnival Calabar
spotlight.kicker: Every December since 2004
spotlight.description: Each December, Calabar gives its streets over to a month of festival that builds to the carnival parade after Christmas. Competing bands dance a long route through the city in costumes built around a yearly theme, with floats and music. Governor Donald Duke launched it in 2004 to make the state a destination, and it is billed as Africa's Biggest Street Party.

foods.name: Edikang ikong
foods.description: A rich soup dense with fluted pumpkin leaves and waterleaf, cooked with meat, dried fish and periwinkle in palm oil.

foods.name: Afang soup
foods.description: Finely shredded afang (okazi) leaves and waterleaf with meat and seafood. Shared with neighbouring Akwa Ibom.

foods.name: Ekpang nkukwo
foods.description: Grated cocoyam and water yam wrapped in tender cocoyam leaves and simmered with periwinkle, fish and palm oil.

foods.name: Afia efere
foods.description: A pale, peppery "white soup" made without palm oil, usually with goat or chicken, served with pounded yam.

crafts: The Ikom monoliths: carved standing stones with faces and inscriptions, arranged in circles around Alok and nearby villages.
Nsibidi: a system of signs used by the Ejagham and their neighbours, and by the Ekpe society, drawn on cloth, walls, calabashes and skin.
Beadwork and raffia work made for dress and ceremony.
states.attire: Efik women are known for the ọnyọnyọ, a long flowing gown worn with coral beads. Efik men wear the usobo wrapper with a long white shirt and a broad neck scarf, the ọkpọmkpọm. Each of the state's other peoples has its own dress.

places.name: Obudu Mountain Resort
places.description: A highland retreat on the plateau, reached by a long winding road or a cable car.

places.name: Cross River National Park
places.description: Two tracts of protected rainforest, Oban and Okwangwo, sheltering the Cross River gorilla, drills and forest elephants.

places.name: Afi Mountain Wildlife Sanctuary
places.description: Forest reserve and home of the Drill Ranch, a primate rehabilitation centre.

places.name: Agbokim Waterfalls
places.description: A fan of cascades dropping into forest near the Cameroon border.

places.name: Kwa Falls
places.description: A waterfall in a narrow gorge of the Great Kwa River.

places.name: Ikom monoliths, Alok
places.description: The best-known group of carved stones, kept as an open-air museum.

places.name: Old Residency Museum, Calabar
places.description: The National Museum, in a prefabricated colonial building, on the history of Old Calabar.

history.event: Old Calabar is a major port, first in the Atlantic slave trade and later in palm oil, with Efik merchant houses as middlemen.
Scottish Presbyterian missionaries arrive in Calabar.
Calabar becomes the seat of the Oil Rivers Protectorate, later the Niger Coast Protectorate.
South-Eastern State is created on 27 May, with Calabar as capital.
The state is renamed Cross River.
Akwa Ibom State is carved out.
The first Carnival Calabar is held.
Nigeria hands the Bakassi Peninsula to Cameroon, following a 2002 judgment of the International Court of Justice.

notableFigures.name: Eyo Ita (1903–1972)
notableFigures.note: Educator and politician who founded the West African People's Institute in Calabar. Born at Ibeno, now in Akwa Ibom State.

notableFigures.name: Margaret Ekpo (1914–2006)
notableFigures.note: Women's rights activist and politician, born in Creek Town.

notableFigures.name: Hogan "Kid" Bassey (1932–1998)
notableFigures.note: Boxer from Calabar. World featherweight champion in 1957.

notableFigures.name: Donald Duke (born 1961)
notableFigures.note: Governor from 1999 to 2007, who launched the carnival.

didYouKnow: The Cross River gorilla, found only along this stretch of the Nigeria–Cameroon border, is the rarest great ape in Africa. A few hundred survive.
Calabar was the seat of the protectorate government before the capital moved to Lagos in 1906.
Nsibidi signs were in use here long before the Latin alphabet arrived.
The Hope Waddell Training Institution in Calabar, founded in 1895, is one of the oldest secondary schools in Nigeria.

states.name: Delta
states.createdNote: Created on 27 August 1991, when Bendel State was divided into Delta and Edo.

population.source: National Population Commission / National Bureau of Statistics projection

states.terrain: The western half of the Niger Delta and the plain behind it. Along the coast and up the Forcados, Escravos, Benin and Warri rivers, the land is a tidal maze of mangrove creeks and low islands. Behind the mangrove lies freshwater swamp, flooded each year when the Niger rises. Further north and east the ground is a drier, gently rising plain that ends at the bank of the Niger at Asaba.
states.climate: Hot, humid and wet, with well over 2,000 mm of rain a year on the coast and somewhat less inland. The rains run from about March to October.
states.vegetation: Mangrove forest in the tidal south-west, freshwater swamp forest along the rivers, and lowland rainforest inland, much of it now farmland, rubber and oil palm.
peoples: Urhobo, the largest single group, in the centre of the state
Ijaw (Izon), in the creeks of the south and west
Itsekiri, around Warri and the Benin River
Anioma, the Igbo-speaking peoples of the north and east: Enuani (Aniocha and Oshimili), Ika and Ukwuani (Ndokwa)
languages: Igbo, in its Enuani, Ika and Ukwuani forms
English and Nigerian Pidgin, of which the Warri variety is famous

spotlight.title: Udje
spotlight.kicker: Song, dance and satire among the Urhobo
spotlight.description: Udje is a tradition of sung poetry and dance among the Urhobo, a battle of songs. Rival quarters or towns composed songs about each other, picking over real scandals, failings and misfortunes with humour, caricature and merciless detail, and kept both songs and dance steps secret until the day of the performance. The colonial courts tried to suppress it with stiff penalties. Composers and lead singers became famous, and the best songs are still remembered. Udje is one tradition among many in a state where every people has its own festivals.

foods.name: Banga soup and starch
foods.description: A soup of palm fruit extract with fresh fish or meat and a distinct blend of spices, eaten with a stretchy, golden swallow made from cassava starch and palm oil.

foods.name: Owho soup
foods.description: A smooth, yellow soup of palm oil thickened with starch or garri and set with potash, served with boiled yam, plantain or starch.

foods.name: Ukodo
foods.description: Yam and unripe plantain cooked in a pepper-soup broth with goat meat or fish. Breakfast, comfort and ceremony in one pot.

foods.name: Fresh fish pepper soup
foods.description: Catfish or tilapia from the rivers in a hot, thin broth.

crafts: Akwa ocha: a handwoven white cloth of the Anioma people, worn for weddings, titles and ceremonies.
Wood sculpture: the shrine figures of Urhobo carvers are widely collected.
Canoe building and the weaving of fish traps in the riverine areas.
states.attire: Dress varies by people. Urhobo, Isoko and Itsekiri men often wear a long shirt with a wrapper, a hat and a walking stick, and women a blouse with two wrappers, a head tie and coral beads. Among the Anioma, white akwa ocha cloth marks great occasions.

places.name: Source of the River Ethiope, Umuaja
places.description: A clear spring that rises at the foot of a giant silk-cotton tree and becomes a river.

places.name: Nana Living History Museum, Koko
places.description: The palace of the 19th-century Itsekiri merchant chief Nana Olomu, with his belongings.

states.name: Ebonyi
states.createdNote: Created on 1 October 1996 from parts of Enugu State (Abakaliki) and Abia State (Afikpo).

population.source: National Population Commission / National Bureau of Statistics projection

states.terrain: Low, gently rolling plains in the basin of the Cross River, which runs along the eastern edge. The ground rises to low hills around Afikpo in the south.
states.climate: Humid and tropical, with about eight months of rain and a dry season of about four.
states.vegetation: Forest–savanna mosaic across most of the state, with forest in the far south. Wide tracts are under rice and yam.
peoples: Igbo, in several distinct peoples: Izzi, Ezza, Ikwo and Ngbo in the north, and Afikpo, Edda, Okposi and Uburu in the south, among others
Orring, who speak Korring, in communities such as Ntezi, Okpoto and Effium
Communities speaking Kukele, Legbo and Mbembe, languages of the Cross River family, along the eastern border
languages: Igbo, in dialects that differ markedly between north and south

spotlight.title: The salt lakes of Okposi and Uburu
spotlight.kicker: Why Ebonyi is the Salt of the Nation
spotlight.description: At Okposi and Uburu, in the south of the state, brine rises into shallow lakes. For centuries the women of the two towns have drawn the salt water and boiled it down in large pots to make salt, a trade that once reached markets across the region. Custom reserves the work for women and sets rules about who may enter the lake. During the civil war, when imported salt was cut off, these lakes helped supply Biafra. The state takes its slogan from them.

foods.name: Abakaliki rice
foods.description: Locally grown rice, parboiled and milled at Abakaliki's great rice mill. Sold across Nigeria and prized for its flavour.

foods.name: Ji
foods.description: Yam, the pride of the farmers of the northern plains: boiled, roasted with palm oil, or pounded and eaten with soup.

crafts: Salt-making at Okposi and Uburu, by boiling brine in clay pots.
Mask carving: Afikpo is known for its carved ceremonial masks.
states.attire: Igbo dress in local forms: wrappers with a tunic or blouse, caps and head ties, and beads for occasions. The Orring and other communities have their own traditions of dress.

places.name: Okposi and Uburu salt lakes
places.description: The brine lakes and the salt-makers' working places beside them.

places.name: Abakaliki Rice Mill

places.name: Unwana and Ndibe beaches, Afikpo

places.name: Abakaliki Green Lake
places.description: A small lake on the edge of the capital.

states.name: Edo
states.createdNote: Created on 27 August 1991, when Bendel State was divided into Edo and Delta.

population.source: National Population Commission / National Bureau of Statistics projection

states.terrain: The land rises from south to north. The south is a low, sandy plain around Benin City, which in the far south-west reaches the swamps and creeks at the edge of the Niger Delta. The centre is the Esan plateau. The north is hill country, with bare granite ridges around Igarra and Somorika. The Niger forms a short stretch of the eastern border.
states.climate: Tropical. The south is humid, with rain from about March to October. The north is drier, with a longer dry season.
states.vegetation: Lowland rainforest in the south, part of it protected in Okomu National Park and much of the rest planted with rubber and oil palm. Forest–savanna mosaic and open woodland in the north. Freshwater swamp and some mangrove in the far south-west.
highlands: Somorika and Igarra hills, in Akoko-Edo
peoples: Edo (Bini), in and around Benin City
The peoples of Akoko-Edo, among them the Okpameri and the Etuno of Igarra
Ijaw, in the creeks of the south-west

spotlight.title: The Igue Festival
spotlight.kicker: Benin City, every December
spotlight.description: Igue is the festival of the Oba of Benin, held between Christmas and the New Year. Over seven days the Oba gives thanks for the year past and blesses the land and the people, in ceremonies that also honour the Obas before him. The chiefs come to the palace in full regalia to dance and pay homage. It closes with the Ewere rite, a blessing for the year to come. The festival is traced to the reign of Oba Ewuare in the 15th century.

foods.name: Black soup
foods.description: A dark, fragrant soup made from ground bitterleaf, scent leaf and other greens, cooked with meat, dried fish and palm oil. Called omoebe in Edo.

foods.name: Owo soup
foods.description: A smooth golden sauce of palm oil set with potash, eaten with boiled yam or plantain. Shared with the peoples of Delta State.

foods.name: Omi ukpoka
foods.description: Corn soup: ground maize cooked with smoked fish and leafy vegetables. A dish of the Afemai north.

foods.name: Pounded yam
foods.description: Eaten with black soup, ogbono or egusi, across the state.

crafts: Bronze and brass casting: the guild of casters on Igun Street in Benin City has worked for the Oba for centuries and still casts by the lost-wax method.
Ivory and wood carving, by the carvers' guild of the Benin court.
Coral beadwork: crowns, collars and garments of red coral for the Oba, chiefs and brides.
states.attire: In Benin, red coral beads are the mark of rank and of great occasions. Brides wear the okuku, a crown of coral beads worked into the hair, with a wrapper of velvet or other rich cloth. Men wear a wrapper with a shirt and strings of beads. The Esan, Afemai, Owan and other peoples have their own dress and cloths.

states.name: Ekiti
states.createdNote: Carved out of Ondo State on 1 October 1996.

population.source: National Population Commission / National Bureau of Statistics projection

states.terrain: Upland country, almost all of it more than 250 metres above sea level, built on old hard rock that breaks the surface in steep, bare-sided hills. The main groups stand around Ikere-Ekiti in the south, Efon-Alaaye on the western edge and Ado-Ekiti in the centre.
states.climate: Tropical, with a rainy season from about April to October and a dry season from November to March.
states.vegetation: Rainforest in the south, thinning to savanna woodland in the north. Much of the forest is farmed for cocoa, yam and rice.
peoples: Ekiti, a Yoruba people made up of many historic kingdoms, each with its own ruler and dialect
Akoko and Yagba communities near the eastern and northern borders
Residents from other parts of Nigeria, mostly in Ado-Ekiti and the larger towns

spotlight.title: Udiroko
spotlight.kicker: Ado-Ekiti's new year festival
spotlight.description: Udiroko is the great annual festival of Ado-Ekiti. It marks the start of the year in the town's traditional calendar, and it is the day the people of Ado gather before the Ewi, their king, to pay homage, give thanks for the year past and pray for the one ahead. Chiefs, quarters, age groups and families arrive in turn with drumming and dance, and sons and daughters of the town come home for it. The festival is held in August.

foods.name: Iyán
foods.description: Pounded yam: boiled yam worked in a mortar until smooth and stretchy. Ekiti is yam country, and iyán is the dish the state is known for across Nigeria.

foods.name: Ẹ̀fọ́ rírò
foods.description: A rich stew of leafy greens with pepper, locust bean, palm oil, meat and dried fish. The usual partner for iyán.

foods.name: Igbemo rice
foods.description: Unpolished local rice grown around Igbemo-Ekiti, with a nutty taste and a firmer bite than imported rice.

states.name: Enugu

population.source: National Population Commission / National Bureau of Statistics projection

states.terrain: The Udi–Nsukka Plateau runs north to south through the state and ends in a steep, east-facing escarpment above the city of Enugu. East of the scarp the land drops to the plains of the Cross River basin.
states.climate: Tropical wet and dry. Rain falls from about April to October, followed by a dry season with harmattan in December and January.
states.vegetation: Forest–savanna mosaic: grassland and farmland on the plateau, with rainforest surviving in the valleys and the south.
peoples: Igbo, in several distinct communities and dialect areas, including Nsukka, Nkanu, Udi and Awgu
An Igala-speaking community at Ette in Igbo-Eze North
Residents from across Nigeria, especially in Enugu city

spotlight.title: The New Yam Festival
spotlight.kicker: Ịwa ji, between August and October
spotlight.description: Across Igboland the yam harvest opens with thanksgiving, and nobody eats the new crop before it. Each town in Enugu State keeps its own day, usually between August and October. The eldest man or the traditional ruler offers the first tubers, then cuts and tastes the new yam before anyone else. After that the town feasts: roasted yam with palm oil, visiting between compounds, dance troupes and masquerades in the square. It is a harvest rite, a homecoming and a new year in one.

foods.name: Ọkpa
foods.description: A firm, golden pudding of Bambara groundnut flour, palm oil and pepper, steamed in leaves. Travellers buy it warm at Ninth Mile.

foods.name: Abacha
foods.description: Shredded dried cassava dressed with palm oil, ugba (fermented oil bean), garden egg and crayfish. Served at any gathering.

foods.name: Achicha with fio fio
foods.description: Dried cocoyam steamed until soft and tossed with pigeon peas, palm oil and leaves. A dish of the dry season.

foods.name: Yam and fio fio
foods.description: A pottage of yam with pigeon peas, served with palm oil and pepper sauce. A favourite across the state.

crafts: Uli: a drawing tradition of Igbo women, painted on skin and on walls in flowing lines and spare motifs. From the 1970s artists at the University of Nigeria, Nsukka built a modern school of painting on it.
Masquerade arts: carved masks and layered costumes made for mmanwụ performances, with distinct traditions in the Nsukka area.
states.attire: Men often wear the isiagu, a tunic printed with lion heads, with a wrapper or trousers and a cap; titled men wear red caps. Women wear a blouse with two wrappers and a head tie, with beads for occasions. This is dress shared across Igboland, not Enugu's alone.

states.name: Federal Capital Territory
states.createdNote: A federal territory, not a state. It was created on 3 February 1976 from parts of the then Niger, Plateau, Kwara and Kaduna states, most of it from Niger, and became the seat of government on 12 December 1991. Its six local units are called area councils.

population.source: National Population Commission / National Bureau of Statistics projection
population.note: The 2006 census counted 1,406,239. The territory has grown faster than any state since.

states.terrain: Rolling savanna in the centre of the country, a little north of the Niger–Benue confluence. Hills and ridges cross the north and east, and bare domes of granite stand above the plain. The best known is Aso Rock, about 400 metres high, at the foot of which the central city is built.
states.climate: Tropical savanna. The rains run from about April to October. The hottest months are from January to April, and December is the coolest, with harmattan haze.
states.vegetation: Guinea savanna woodland and grassland, with forest along the streams. Much of it is now city, suburb and farmland.
peoples: Gbagyi, the largest of the peoples who lived here before the capital was built
People from every state in Nigeria, who now make up most of the population
languages: English and Hausa, as common languages

spotlight.title: A capital built on purpose
spotlight.kicker: Why Abuja is a territory and not a state
spotlight.description: Abuja did not grow. It was decided. By the 1970s Lagos was badly congested, hemmed in by lagoon and sea with little room to expand, and it was at once the federal capital, a state capital and the country's main port. In 1975 a panel under Justice Akinola Aguda recommended a new capital at the centre of the country, easy to reach from every part of it and on land not identified with any of the three largest ethnic groups. The territory was created in 1976 and a master plan drawn up in 1979. The government moved in on 12 December 1991. The Federal Capital Territory belongs to the federation as a whole. It has no governor: a minister appointed by the President runs it, the National Assembly makes its laws, and its six area councils have elected chairmen.

foods.name: Suya
foods.description: Skewered beef grilled over charcoal with yaji spice. Every district has its famous spot, and the queues form at dusk.

foods.name: Grilled fish
foods.description: Whole fish chosen from the tank, grilled over coals and served with pepper sauce and chips or plantain, at open-air fish spots around the city.

foods.name: Kilishi and masa
foods.description: Dried spiced beef and fried rice cakes, brought by the city's northern neighbours.

foods.name: The whole country's kitchen
foods.description: Abuja's own cooking is whatever its people brought with them. The food of the Gbagyi and other first peoples of the territory is still to be recorded here.

crafts: Pottery: the Gbagyi are celebrated potters, and Ladi Kwali, from Kwali, became the most famous potter in Africa.
The Abuja Arts and Crafts Village, where makers from all over the country sell their work.
Pottery villages at Ushafa and Bwari.
states.attire: As the capital, Abuja wears the dress of every Nigerian people. The Gbagyi and the territory's other first peoples have their own cloths and festival dress, still to be described here from local sources.

places.name: Aso Rock
places.description: The great granite dome behind the Three Arms Zone, where the Presidency, the National Assembly and the Supreme Court stand.

places.name: National Mosque and National Christian Centre
places.description: The two national places of worship, facing each other across the central district.

places.name: Millennium Park
places.description: The city's largest park, opened in 2003.

places.name: Abuja Arts and Crafts Village
places.description: Thatched huts of craft stalls in the middle of the city.

places.name: Jabi Lake
places.description: A reservoir with a lakeside park.

places.name: Usuma Dam and Ushafa
places.description: The city's reservoir in the Bwari hills, near a village of potters.

history.event: The Aguda panel recommends a new capital in the centre of the country.
The Federal Capital Territory is created on 3 February. It takes its name from the nearby emirate town of Abuja, which is renamed Suleja.
The master plan for the city, by International Planning Associates, is completed. The Japanese architect Kenzo Tange designs the central district.
The first districts, roads and public buildings are built.
On 12 December the seat of government moves from Lagos to Abuja.

spotlight.title: Mbari
spotlight.kicker: Houses of art for the earth goddess, in the Owerri country
spotlight.description: When a community around Owerri was called on to honour Ala, the earth goddess, it built a mbari: a sacred house crowded with painted clay figures, some of them life-sized. Ala sat at the centre, and around her the makers modelled gods, ancestors, animals, craftsmen, officials and legendary creatures, a picture of the world as they knew it. The work was sacred and could take years. When the house was finished it was shown to the town's leaders and then left alone to return to the earth, because the making was the offering. Few are built now, but Owerri keeps a Mbari Cultural Centre, and the idea gave its name to the Mbari Club of writers and artists founded in Ibadan in 1961.

spotlight.title: The Nok terracottas
spotlight.kicker: Named after a village in southern Kaduna
spotlight.description: In 1928, tin miners near the village of Nok dug up a small terracotta head. More followed, and from the 1940s the archaeologist Bernard Fagg showed that they belonged to a single ancient culture spread across central Nigeria. Nok sculptors modelled human heads and figures in fired clay, some nearly life-sized, with stylised features, elaborate hairstyles and careful detail of beads and dress. The culture flourished from around 1500 BC to about the turn of the era, and its people were working iron by about the middle of the first millennium BC. Outside ancient Egypt, Nok terracottas are the earliest large figurative sculpture known in Africa.

spotlight.title: The Kano Durbar
spotlight.kicker: Hawan Sallah, at Eid al-Fitr and Eid al-Adha
spotlight.description: For several days after each Eid, the Emir of Kano rides out with his court. District heads and their mounted regiments follow in embroidered robes and turbans, their horses dressed in quilted and brass-studded regalia, with drummers, trumpeters and lancers between them. Each day's ride has a name and a route, among them Hawan Sallah, Hawan Daushe and Hawan Nassarawa. At the palace the horsemen pay homage with the jahi: a full gallop toward the Emir, pulled up at the last moment with swords raised in salute. UNESCO added the Kano Durbar to its Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2024.

spotlight.title: Daura and the legend of Bayajidda
spotlight.kicker: Where the Hausa states begin their story
spotlight.description: Every Hausa child knows the story. A stranger named Bayajidda came to Daura and found the town unable to draw water, because a great snake lived in the well and allowed it only on Fridays. He killed the snake, and the queen, Daurama, married him. Their son's sons went out to rule seven towns, the Hausa Bakwai: Daura, Kano, Katsina, Zazzau, Gobir, Rano and Biram. In Daura you can still be shown the Kusugu well, and the emirate is honoured as the oldest of the Hausa states.

states.name: Kebbi
states.createdNote: Carved out of Sokoto State on 27 August 1991.

states.terrain: Wide river plains and the country between them. The Rima and the Niger cross the state, and their floodplains, called fadama, are flooded each year and farmed as the water falls. The north is flat and sandy. The south, around Zuru, is rocky hill country. At Yauri the Niger widens into the upper end of Kainji Lake.

spotlight.title: The Argungu Fishing Festival
spotlight.kicker: One hour in the Matan Fada river
spotlight.description: At a signal, thousands of men run into the river at Argungu with hand nets and large gourds. They have one hour to bring out the biggest fish they can, using only traditional tools or their bare hands. The winning catch can weigh as much as a man. The festival was first held in 1934 to mark the end of centuries of hostility between the Sokoto Caliphate and the kingdom of Kebbi, and it has grown into days of boat races, wrestling, music and a great agricultural show. UNESCO placed it on its Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2016.

states.name: Kogi
states.createdNote: Created on 27 August 1991 from parts of Kwara and Benue states.

population.source: National Population Commission / National Bureau of Statistics projection

states.terrain: The state is built around a meeting of rivers. The Niger comes down from the north-west and the Benue from the east, and they join at Lokoja and flow south as one. West of the Niger the land is hilly, with rocky ridges around Okene and Kabba, and Mount Patti stands directly above Lokoja. East of the river is the lower, rolling Igala country.
states.climate: Tropical, with rain from about April to October, 1,100 to 1,300 mm in a year, and a dry season with harmattan from November to March. Lokoja is one of the hottest towns in Nigeria.

spotlight.title: The confluence at Lokoja
spotlight.kicker: Where the Niger meets the Benue
spotlight.description: Nigeria's two great rivers meet at Lokoja. From the top of Mount Patti you can see the whole of it: the Niger arriving from the north-west, the Benue from the east, and the two running side by side in different shades for some distance before they blend and turn south for the sea. This is the Y at the centre of the map, and the reason the country has the shape it does. Lokoja grew up at the meeting point. British expeditions set up a farm and then a trading settlement here in the 19th century, and on 1 January 1900 the Protectorate of Northern Nigeria was proclaimed in the town, which served as its first capital.

foods.name: River fish pepper soup

foods.name: Pounded yam

spotlight.title: The soapstone figures of Esie
spotlight.kicker: A thousand carvings and no one knows who made them
spotlight.description: In the Igbomina town of Esie stands the largest collection of soapstone sculpture in Africa: something like a thousand figures of men and women, most of them seated, some kneeling, wearing beads and elaborate hairstyles and holding staffs, cutlasses or musical instruments. Local tradition says a hunter found them gathered in the bush long ago. Nobody has established who carved them or when. The people of Esie adopted them and held a yearly festival in their honour, and in 1945 a museum was built to house them, the first museum in Nigeria.

states.name: Lagos

population.source: National Population Commission / National Bureau of Statistics projection
population.note: The Lagos State Government publishes far higher estimates, above 20 million. The 2006 census counted 9,113,605.

states.terrain: A low coastal plain threaded with lagoons, creeks and sandy barrier islands. Close to a quarter of the state is water, and much of the city stands on land reclaimed from it.
states.climate: Tropical monsoon. Rain falls from about April to October, easing briefly in August. The dry season brings harmattan haze between December and February.

peoples: Ijebu, mainly around Ikorodu and Epe

spotlight.title: The Eyo Festival
spotlight.kicker: Adamu Orisa Play, Lagos Island
spotlight.description: Eyo (Ẹ̀yọ̀) belongs to Lagos Island. On the day, thousands of masquerades in flowing white robes and wide-brimmed hats (aga) fill the streets of Isale Eko, each carrying a tall staff called the opambata, and process to Tafawa Balewa Square. The festival has no fixed date. It is staged to honour a departed Oba or an eminent Lagosian, or to mark a great occasion. Five senior groups lead the procession: Adimu, Laba, Oniko, Ologede and Agere.

foods.name: Ewa agoyin
foods.description: Beans cooked until they collapse, served under a dark, smoky sauce of dried pepper and palm oil. The name remembers the Togolese and Beninese cooks who first sold it on Lagos streets.

foods.name: Agege bread
foods.description: A soft, dense, slightly sweet white loaf named after the Agege district. The usual partner for ewa agoyin.

foods.name: Party jollof
foods.description: Jollof rice cooked in huge pots over firewood for weddings and owambe parties, prized for the smoky layer at the bottom of the pot.

foods.name: Catfish pepper soup

foods.name: Suya

crafts: Aṣọ ẹbí: families and friends dress in matching cloth for weddings and funerals, which keeps the city's tailors, lace merchants and aṣọ òkè sellers busy.

states.attire: Yoruba dress sets the formal tone: agbádá, bùbá and ṣòkòtò with a fìlà cap for men; ìró and bùbá with a gèlè head tie and ìpèlé shawl for women. In daily life Lagos wears everything, from Ogu and Igbo dress to the Hausa babban riga.

states.name: Nasarawa
states.createdNote: Carved out of Plateau State on 1 October 1996.

population.source: National Population Commission / National Bureau of Statistics projection

states.terrain: The land steps down from north to south. In the north-east it climbs to the edge of the Jos Plateau, where the Farin Ruwa Falls drop down the escarpment, and to the Eggon and Mada hills. The centre is rolling plain. The south is the low valley of the Benue, which forms the southern border.

spotlight.title: The salt of Keana
spotlight.kicker: An old industry of the Alago
spotlight.description: At Keana, in the south of the state, salt-bearing earth and salty water come to the surface in the dry season. For centuries the women of this Alago town have made salt from them. They heap the salty sand in pots, pour pond water through it, and boil the filtered brine until it turns to salt, working from about January to April. Salt from Keana was traded as far as Kano, Sokoto and Borno long before imported salt arrived, and it is still made by hand today. It is one reason the state calls itself the Home of Solid Minerals.

foods.name: Miyar riɗi
foods.description: Beniseed soup: ground sesame cooked with meat or fish and greens. Nasarawa is one of the main sesame-growing states.

Nasarawa adjoins the Federal Capital Territory, and the towns of Karu and Mararaba have become part of greater Abuja.
It was one of six states created on 1 October 1996.
Farin Ruwa means white water.

states.name: Niger
states.createdNote: Created on 3 February 1976, when North-Western State was divided into Niger and Sokoto.

population.source: National Population Commission / National Bureau of Statistics projection

states.terrain: The largest state in the country, shaped by two rivers. The Niger runs along its western and southern sides, held back by the dams at Kainji and Jebba, and the Kaduna crosses the middle to join it. The south is the low, wide Niger valley and the Bida basin. The north and east are higher plains with granite hills, among them Zuma Rock near Suleja.
states.climate: Hot, with rain from about May to October and a dry season with harmattan.
states.vegetation: Guinea savanna woodland across most of the state, with Sudan savanna in the north and grassy floodplains along the rivers.
peoples: Nupe, in the south around Bida
Kambari, Kamuku, Dukawa and Gungawa, in the north-west
The Borgu peoples, around New Bussa

spotlight.title: The craft guilds of Bida
spotlight.kicker: Brass, glass and the Nupe court
spotlight.description: Bida, capital of the Nupe kingdom since the 19th century, is a city of craft quarters. In one, brass-smiths hammer and chase metal into trays, bowls, jugs and goblets. In another, the Masaga glass-makers work molten glass into beads and bangles. Weavers, embroiderers and other craftsmen have their own wards, and each craft is organised as a close-knit guild. The guilds grew up around the court of the Etsu Nupe and have passed their skills down within families ever since.

foods.name: Kuli-kuli
foods.description: Crisp, spiced cakes of ground roasted groundnut. First made by the Nupe, and now eaten across the north and beyond.

foods.name: Rice
foods.description: The Bida basin is one of Nigeria's old rice-growing districts. Local rice is eaten with stew or pounded into tuwo.

foods.name: Fish from the Niger
foods.description: Fresh and smoked fish from Kainji Lake and the river.

foods.name: Masa
foods.description: Fried cakes of fermented rice batter.

crafts: Brasswork and glass beads and bangles, made in Bida.
Nupe embroidery, weaving and carved stools and doors.
Pottery: the Gbagyi tradition made famous by Ladi Kwali, who worked at the pottery centre in Suleja that now bears her name.
states.attire: Nupe men wear wide embroidered gowns and caps, and women wrappers of woven cloth with a head tie. Gbagyi, Hausa, Kambari and other peoples have their own dress.

places.name: Zuma Rock
places.description: A huge dome of rock beside the road to Abuja, shown on the 100-naira note.

places.name: Gurara Falls
places.description: A wide curtain of water on the Gurara River, at its best late in the rains.

places.name: Bida
places.description: The Etsu Nupe's palace and the brass, glass and weaving quarters.

places.name: Kainji Lake National Park
places.description: Nigeria's first national park, shared with Kwara, beside the lake behind Kainji Dam.

places.name: Zungeru
places.description: The ruins of the colonial capital of Northern Nigeria.

places.name: Ladi Kwali Pottery Centre, Suleja
places.description: The workshop where Gbagyi pottery met the studio wheel and kiln.

history.event: By tradition, Tsoede founds the Nupe kingdom.
The explorer Mungo Park dies in the rapids at Bussa.
Bida becomes the capital of the Nupe emirate.
Zungeru is the capital of Northern Nigeria.
Kainji Dam is completed. Old Bussa is flooded and its people move to New Bussa.
Niger State is created on 3 February. The old town of Abuja gives its name to the new federal capital and is renamed Suleja.

notableFigures.name: Abubakar Imam (1911–1981)
notableFigures.note: Writer and editor, born at Kagara. A founder of modern Hausa literature.

notableFigures.name: Ibrahim Babangida (born 1941)
notableFigures.note: Soldier, born in Minna. Head of State from 1985 to 1993.

notableFigures.name: Abdulsalami Abubakar (born 1942)
notableFigures.note: Soldier, born in Minna. Head of State from 1998 to 1999, who handed power to an elected government.

didYouKnow: Niger is the largest state by area.
It is called the Power State, after its hydroelectric dams at Kainji, Jebba and Shiroro.
Nnamdi Azikiwe and Chukwuemeka Odumegwu Ojukwu were both born in Zungeru.
Two of Nigeria's heads of state were born in Minna.
