states.name: Ogun
states.createdNote: Created from the old Western State on 3 February 1976.

population.source: National Population Commission / National Bureau of Statistics projection

states.terrain: Rolling lowland that rises gently northwards, with granite outcrops around Abeokuta, the best known of them Olumo Rock. In the south-east the state reaches the coastal lagoons.
states.climate: Tropical, with a long rainy season from about March to October and a dry season from November to February.
states.vegetation: Lowland rainforest across most of the state, forest–savanna mosaic in the north and west, and mangrove and swamp forest near the coast.
highlands: Olumo Rock and the Abeokuta outcrops
peoples: Ogu (Egun), along the border with the Republic of Benin
Residents from across Nigeria, especially in the towns that border Lagos
languages: Yoruba, in its Egba, Ijebu, Remo, Yewa and Awori dialects

spotlight.title: Ojude Oba
spotlight.kicker: Ijebu-Ode, two days after Eid al-Adha
spotlight.description: Ojude Oba means the king's forecourt. On the third day of Eid al-Adha the people of Ijebu-Ode, of every faith, come before the Awujale, their king, to pay homage. The age-grade societies, called regberegbe, parade group by group in matching cloth chosen and guarded for months beforehand, each trying to outdress the last. Then come the horsemen: the old warrior families ride in on decorated horses to gun salutes and drums. The festival is more than a century old.

foods.name: Ofada rice and ayamase
foods.description: Short-grained, unpolished local rice named after the town of Ofada, served on a leaf with a fierce green-pepper stew of assorted meats and locust bean.

foods.name: Ìkọ́kọrẹ́
foods.description: A pottage of grated water yam cooked with fish, pepper and palm oil. An Ijebu dish.

foods.name: Ebiripo
foods.description: Grated cocoyam wrapped in leaves and steamed, eaten with stew. A dish of the Remo towns.

foods.name: Gari Ijebu
foods.description: Cassava granules fermented longer and roasted finer than most, for a sharp, sour crunch. Soaked in cold water as a snack or made into ẹ̀bà.

foods.name: Lafun
foods.description: A smooth white swallow made from fermented cassava flour, eaten with ewédú and stew in Abeokuta.

crafts: Àdìrẹ: Abeokuta is the home of this indigo resist-dyed cloth. Dyers paint or stencil patterns in cassava paste (àdìrẹ ẹlẹ́kọ), or tie and stitch the cloth (àdìrẹ oníko), before it goes into the dye. Itoku market is the centre of the trade.
states.attire: Yoruba dress: agbádá, bùbá and ṣòkòtò with a fìlà cap for men; ìró and bùbá with a gèlè head tie for women. Àdìrẹ is worn every day and aṣọ òkè on great occasions. The age grades of Ijebu-Ode commission matching outfits each year for Ojude Oba.

places.name: Olumo Rock
places.description: The granite outcrop above Abeokuta where the Egba took refuge in the 19th century. Steps and paths lead to the top and a view across the city.

places.name: Itoku adire market
places.description: Stalls of indigo and many-coloured cloth in the old quarter of Abeokuta.

places.name: Sungbo's Eredo
places.description: A vast system of ramparts and ditches built around the old Ijebu kingdom, among the largest earthworks in Africa.

places.name: Bilikisu Sungbo shrine, Oke-Eri
places.description: A grove near Ijebu-Ode honoured as the burial place of the woman said to have ordered the Eredo built.

places.name: Ake, Abeokuta
places.description: The palace of the Alake of Egbaland and the nearby Cathedral Church of St Peter, whose first church was begun in the 1840s and is often called the oldest in Nigeria.

places.name: Olusegun Obasanjo Presidential Library
places.description: A museum, archive and park in Abeokuta.

history.event: Egba refugees from the wars that followed the fall of Oyo settle beneath Olumo Rock and found Abeokuta.
Christian missionaries and freed Yoruba returning from Sierra Leone arrive in Abeokuta.
Iwe Irohin, the first newspaper published in Nigeria, is printed in Abeokuta.
A British expedition defeats the Ijebu kingdom.
The Egba United Government loses its independence and is brought under the new Nigeria.
Women of Abeokuta, led by Funmilayo Ransome-Kuti, protest against taxation without a voice in government. The Alake abdicates in 1949.
Ogun State is created on 3 February.

notableFigures.name: Funmilayo Ransome-Kuti (1900–1978)
notableFigures.note: Teacher and campaigner for women's rights, born in Abeokuta.

notableFigures.name: Obafemi Awolowo (1909–1987)
notableFigures.note: Lawyer and statesman, born in Ikenne. First Premier of the Western Region.

notableFigures.name: Wole Soyinka (born 1934)
notableFigures.note: Playwright and poet, born in Abeokuta. Nobel Prize in Literature, 1986.

notableFigures.name: Olusegun Obasanjo (born 1937)
notableFigures.note: Soldier and statesman from the Abeokuta area. Head of State 1976–1979 and President 1999–2007.

notableFigures.name: Fela Anikulapo Kuti (1938–1997)
notableFigures.note: Musician and creator of Afrobeat, born in Abeokuta.

The first newspaper in Nigeria, Iwe Irohin, was printed in Abeokuta in 1859, in Yoruba.
Ofada rice takes its name from Ofada, a town in the state.
Ogun is called the Gateway State: it borders Lagos and the Republic of Benin, and the main roads north and east from Lagos run through it.

states.name: Ondo
states.createdNote: Created from the old Western State on 3 February 1976. Ekiti was carved out of it in 1996.

population.source: National Population Commission / National Bureau of Statistics projection

states.terrain: The land climbs from south to north. Mangrove creeks and a long Atlantic shore in the Ilaje country give way to forested plains, then to granite hills: the sheer domes of Idanre in the centre and the rocky Akoko country in the north.
states.climate: Tropical, with rain from about March to October. The coast is wetter than the north.
states.vegetation: Mangrove and swamp forest on the coast, rainforest across the centre, much of it planted with cocoa, and savanna woodland in the far north.
peoples: Yoruba peoples, each with its own towns and dialect: Akure, Ondo, Owo, Akoko, Idanre, Ikale and Ilaje
Ijaw: the Arogbo and Apoi, in the creeks of the south-east
Residents from across Nigeria in Akure, Ondo and Ore
languages: Yoruba, in its Akure, Ondo, Owo, Ikale and Ilaje dialects

spotlight.title: The Igogo Festival
spotlight.kicker: Owo, every September and October
spotlight.description: For seventeen days each year the town of Owo remembers Oronsen, the wife of an early king, the Olowo Rerengejen. During the festival the Olowo dresses as a woman and his chiefs plait their hair, and they dance through the town. Drumming is forbidden for the whole period, and men do not wear caps before the king; the dancers keep time by striking buffalo horns together. The festival is said to be more than 600 years old.

foods.name: Pupuru
foods.description: Cassava fermented, pressed and dried over a wood fire, then turned in hot water into a firm, smoky swallow. A staple of the Ikale and Ilaje country.

foods.name: Iyán
foods.description: Pounded yam, eaten with ẹ̀fọ́ rírò, ẹ̀gúsí or okra soup. As central here as in Ekiti.

foods.name: Asun
foods.description: Goat meat grilled over an open fire, then chopped and tossed with onion and a great deal of pepper. A Yoruba dish loved across the south-west.

foods.name: Fresh fish pepper soup
foods.description: Fish from the Ilaje creeks and coast in a thin, hot broth.

crafts: Owo art: terracotta sculptures of the 15th century, excavated in the town around 1970, and a long tradition of ivory carving link Owo to both Ife and Benin.
states.attire: Yoruba dress across most of the state: agbádá, bùbá and ṣòkòtò with a fìlà cap for men; ìró and bùbá with a gèlè head tie for women. Coral beads mark chiefs in Owo, where court dress shows the town's old ties to Benin. The Ijaw communities of the south-east have their own dress.

places.name: Idanre Hills
places.description: A cluster of sheer granite domes above Idanre town. A long flight of steps climbs to the old settlement on top, which was lived in until the 1920s.

places.name: Owo Museum and the Olowo's palace
places.description: A museum of Owo terracottas and ivories, beside one of the largest palace compounds in Yorubaland.

places.name: Iho Eleru, Isarun
places.description: The "cave of ashes", a rock shelter where a human skeleton more than 11,000 years old was excavated in 1965.

places.name: Deji's palace, Akure
places.description: The old palace of the king of Akure, a national monument.

places.name: Araromi beach
places.description: A stretch of Atlantic shore in the Ilaje country.

history.event: People are living at Iho Eleru, near Akure. The burial found there is among the oldest human remains known from West Africa.
Owo's sculptors are working in terracotta and ivory.
Ondo State is created on 3 February, with Akure as capital.
Ekiti State is carved out.

notableFigures.name: D. O. Fagunwa (1903–1963)
notableFigures.note: Novelist from Oke-Igbo, whose Ògbójú Ọdẹ nínú Igbó Irúnmọlẹ̀ (1938) is a founding work of the novel in Yoruba.

notableFigures.name: Adekunle Ajasin (1908–1997)
notableFigures.note: Teacher and politician from Owo. First civilian governor of Ondo State.

notableFigures.name: Gani Fawehinmi (1938–2009)
notableFigures.note: Lawyer and human rights campaigner from Ondo town.

notableFigures.name: King Sunny Ade (born 1946)
notableFigures.note: Jùjú musician, of a royal family of Ondo town.

The skeleton from Iho Eleru is more than 11,000 years old.

states.name: Osun
states.createdNote: Carved out of Oyo State on 27 August 1991.

population.source: National Population Commission / National Bureau of Statistics projection

states.terrain: Gently rolling upland, rising to forested hills in the east around Ilesa and the border with Ekiti. The state is named for the River Osun, which crosses it from north-east to south-west.
states.climate: Tropical, with rain from about March or April to October and a dry season from November.
states.vegetation: Lowland rainforest across most of the state, much of it farmed for cocoa and kola, and forest–savanna mosaic in the north.
highlands: Ijesa hills, around Ilesa and Erin-Ijesa
peoples: Yoruba peoples: Ife, Ijesa, Oyo, Igbomina and Ibolo, each centred on its own towns
Long-settled communities from other parts of Nigeria in Osogbo, Ile-Ife and Ilesa
languages: Yoruba, in its Ife, Ijesa, Oyo and Igbomina dialects

spotlight.title: The Osun-Osogbo Festival
spotlight.kicker: Osogbo, every August
spotlight.description: Each August the people of Osogbo renew the bond between their town and Osun, the goddess of the river on whose bank it was founded. After two weeks of rites, the Arugbá, a young woman of the royal house, carries a calabash of offerings from the palace of the Ataoja to the river, through the Osun-Osogbo Sacred Grove, with the whole town and thousands of visitors behind her. The grove is one of the last stretches of sacred high forest left in Yorubaland. From the 1950s the Austrian-born artist Susanne Wenger and local artists rebuilt its shrines and filled it with sculpture. UNESCO made it a World Heritage Site in 2005.

foods.name: Dòdò Ikire
foods.description: Very ripe plantain mashed with pepper and salt, shaped into balls and fried dark in palm oil. The roadside snack that made the town of Ikire famous.

foods.name: Iyán and ẹ̀fọ́ rírò
foods.description: Pounded yam with a rich stew of greens, pepper, locust bean and assorted meats. The favourite of the Ijesa towns.

foods.name: Àmàlà with ewédú and gbẹ̀gìrì
foods.description: Dark yam-flour swallow with jute-leaf and bean soups, eaten across the Oyo-speaking west of the state.

crafts: The art of Ife: between about the 12th and 15th centuries the artists of Ile-Ife made naturalistic heads and figures in copper alloy and terracotta that rank among the great sculpture of the world.
The Osogbo school: workshops held in the town in the 1960s launched a generation of painters, printmakers and sculptors, and the town is still full of studios and galleries.
Àdìrẹ: Osogbo is an old centre of indigo dyeing.
states.attire: Yoruba dress: agbádá, bùbá and ṣòkòtò with a fìlà cap for men; ìró and bùbá with a gèlè head tie for women, in àdìrẹ for every day and aṣọ òkè for occasions. White is worn by devotees of Osun at the festival.

places.name: Osun-Osogbo Sacred Grove
places.description: Forest, river, shrines and sculpture on the edge of Osogbo. A UNESCO World Heritage Site.

places.name: Ile-Ife
places.description: The city the Yoruba hold to be their place of origin, with the palace of the Ooni, the Ife museum and the tall granite Staff of Oranmiyan.

places.name: Erin-Ijesa Waterfalls
places.description: Also called Olumirin: a waterfall that drops in seven steps through forest.

places.name: Obafemi Awolowo University
places.description: A campus at Ile-Ife admired for its modern architecture.

places.name: Osogbo galleries
places.description: Studios and galleries of the Osogbo artists, among them the Nike Centre for Art and Culture.

history.event: Ile-Ife is a wealthy city. Its artists cast heads in copper alloy and model them in terracotta.
At Osogbo, an Ibadan army defeats the cavalry of Ilorin and halts its advance into the south.
The Kiriji War, fought largely in the hills of the Ijesa and Ekiti country.
A hoard of copper-alloy heads is dug up at Wunmonije Compound in Ile-Ife.
The University of Ife is founded. It is renamed Obafemi Awolowo University in 1987.
Osun State is created on 27 August from Oyo State.
The Osun-Osogbo Sacred Grove becomes a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

notableFigures.name: Bola Ige (1930–2001)
notableFigures.note: Lawyer and politician from Esa-Oke. Governor of the old Oyo State and later Attorney-General of the Federation.

notableFigures.name: Duro Ladipo (1931–1978)
notableFigures.note: Dramatist from Osogbo, best known for the Yoruba opera Ọba Kò So.

notableFigures.name: Enoch Adeboye (born 1942)
notableFigures.note: Pastor and former mathematics lecturer, from Ifewara.

notableFigures.name: Jimoh Buraimoh (born 1943)
notableFigures.note: Painter from Osogbo, known for his bead paintings.

didYouKnow: In Yoruba the name is written Ọ̀ṣun, after the river and its goddess.
Ile-Ife is held by the Yoruba to be the place where the world began.
Nigeria has two World Heritage Sites. The Osun-Osogbo grove is one; the other is the Sukur Cultural Landscape in Adamawa.
With 30 local government areas, Osun has more than any other state in the South West except Oyo.

states.name: Oyo
states.createdNote: Created from the old Western State on 3 February 1976. Osun was carved out of it in 1991.

population.source: National Population Commission / National Bureau of Statistics projection

states.terrain: Broad plains of old hard rock that rise gently northwards, studded with dome-shaped granite hills. Ibadan is built over a line of ridges; the open Oke-Ogun country stretches north-west to the border with the Republic of Benin.
states.climate: Tropical, with rain from about April to October and a dry season from November to March. The north is drier than the south.
states.vegetation: Rainforest in the south around Ibadan, now mostly farmland and city, passing into forest–savanna mosaic and open Guinea savanna in the north.
peoples: Yoruba peoples: Oyo, Ibadan, Ogbomoso, Ibarapa and the towns of Oke-Ogun
Fulani herding communities, mainly in Oke-Ogun and Ibarapa
Hausa, Igbo and many other communities in Ibadan, some settled for generations
languages: Yoruba. The Oyo dialect is the basis of the standard written language.

spotlight.title: The Ṣàngó Festival
spotlight.kicker: Oyo town, every August
spotlight.description: Ṣàngó was an Alaafin of the old Oyo Empire who is honoured as the òrìṣà of thunder and lightning. Every August, for about ten days, his devotees gather in Oyo town, at the palace of the Alaafin and the Koso shrine. There is bàtá drumming, praise chanting, dance and displays by the Ẹlẹ́gùn Ṣàngó, the mediums of the god, dressed in red. Worshippers come from across Yorubaland and from Brazil, Cuba and the Caribbean, where Ṣàngó has been honoured for centuries. UNESCO added the festival to its Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2023.

foods.name: Àmàlà and abula
foods.description: A dark, soft swallow of yam flour under two soups poured together, ewédú (jute leaf) and gbẹ̀gìrì (bean), with pepper stew and assorted meats. Ibadan's canteens are judged by it.

foods.name: Wàrà
foods.description: Soft fresh cheese made from cow's milk by Fulani women, sold in rounds and often fried.

foods.name: Ọ̀lẹ̀lẹ̀
foods.description: Steamed bean pudding with pepper, oil and fish or egg, known elsewhere as moin-moin.

foods.name: Ilasa
foods.description: A soup of okra leaves, eaten with àmàlà in Igbo-Ora, where local belief links it to the town's many twins.

crafts: Aṣọ òkè: Iseyin is the best-known home of the Yoruba strip-woven cloth. The three classic kinds are ẹtù (deep indigo), sányán (pale wild silk) and àlàárì (crimson).
Calabash carving in Oyo town, with patterns cut into the dried gourd.
Leatherwork and drum-making in Oyo town, including the dùndún talking drum.
states.attire: Yoruba dress: agbádá, bùbá and ṣòkòtò with a fìlà cap for men; ìró and bùbá with a gèlè head tie for women. For weddings and chieftaincy the cloth is aṣọ òkè, and families often dress alike. Fulani and other communities keep their own dress.

places.name: Old Oyo National Park
places.description: Savanna woodland in the north of the state, with the ruins of Oyo-Ile, capital of the Oyo Empire.

places.name: Alaafin's palace, Oyo
places.description: The seat of the Alaafin since the kingdom moved south in the 19th century.

places.name: Mapo Hall, Ibadan
places.description: A colonial-era town hall on a hill at the centre of old Ibadan.

places.name: University of Ibadan
places.description: Nigeria's first university, founded in 1948, with a campus of notable mid-century buildings.

places.name: Cocoa House, Ibadan
places.description: A tower completed in 1965 with the earnings of the cocoa trade, and for years the tallest building in Nigeria.

places.name: Ado-Awaye and Iyake Lake
places.description: A climb up a granite hill to a small lake held near the summit.

states.name: Plateau
states.createdNote: Created on 3 February 1976 from Benue-Plateau State. Nasarawa was carved out of it in 1996.

population.source: National Population Commission / National Bureau of Statistics projection

states.terrain: The north of the state is the Jos Plateau, a block of high, open country more than 1,200 metres above sea level, studded with granite hills and old volcanic cones. The Shere Hills, east of Jos, reach about 1,829 metres. Rivers that flow to the Niger, the Benue and Lake Chad rise here. To the south the plateau ends in an escarpment, and the land drops to hot lowlands that run down to the Benue plain, where Wase Rock stands alone.
states.climate: The plateau is the coolest inhabited part of Nigeria, with average temperatures between about 13 and 22 °C and cold, dry nights in the harmattan. The southern lowlands are much hotter. Rain falls from about April to October.
states.vegetation: Open grassland with scattered trees on the plateau, much of it farmed, and Guinea savanna woodland in the lowlands.
rivers: Headwaters of the Kaduna, Gongola and Hadejia rivers
peoples: Many more: over 40 groups are counted in the state

spotlight.title: Nzem Berom
spotlight.kicker: One of many festivals on the plateau
spotlight.description: Every people on the plateau keeps its own festival, and together they fill the calendar. Nzem Berom, held around Jos in March or April, gathers several older Berom celebrations of hunting, farming and thanksgiving into one, with music, dance, displays of dress and food, and the Berom ruler, the Gbong Gwom Jos, in attendance. Elsewhere the Ngas keep Pusdung, the Mwaghavul Pus Kat, the Tarok Ilum o'Tarok, and the Goemai and others their own. Each is a homecoming and a statement of who a people are.

states.name: Rivers
states.createdNote: Created on 27 May 1967. Bayelsa was carved out of it in 1996.

population.source: National Population Commission / National Bureau of Statistics projection

states.terrain: The eastern Niger Delta. The southern part of the state is water as much as land: wide estuaries such as the Bonny and New Calabar rivers, tidal creeks walled with mangrove, and sandy barrier islands along the Atlantic. Behind this lies freshwater swamp, and then a drier upland plain on which Port Harcourt and the towns of the north stand. The uplands make up about three-fifths of the state and the riverine areas about two-fifths.
states.climate: Hot, humid and very wet. Rain falls from about March to November, peaking in July, and the coast is far wetter than the north.
states.vegetation: Mangrove forest in the tidal zone, freshwater swamp forest behind it, and lowland rainforest on the uplands, now mostly farmland and oil palm. Oil spills have damaged mangroves and creeks in parts of the state, most seriously in Ogoniland.
peoples: Ikwerre, on the uplands around and north of Port Harcourt
Ijaw peoples of the coast: Kalabari, Okrika (Wakirike), Ibani of Bonny and Opobo, and others
Ogoni: Khana, Gokana, Tai and Eleme
Residents from all over Nigeria in Port Harcourt
languages: About 30 languages and dialects are spoken in the state

spotlight.title: Kalabari masquerade
spotlight.kicker: The water spirits come ashore
spotlight.description: Among the Kalabari, the great art is the masquerade. Each masquerade belongs to a water spirit, the owu, said to live in the creeks, and the Ekine society exists to dance them. A dancer wears a carved headpiece, often a fish, crocodile or other river creature, set flat on top of the head so that its features face the sky and are seen only when he bends forward, over a costume of rich cloth. The performances call on the water spirits for help and guidance. Other peoples of the state have masquerade traditions of their own.

foods.name: Fisherman soup

crafts: Pelete bite: Kalabari women cut and pull threads out of imported checked cloth to leave new patterns of their own design.
Masquerade carving: headpieces in the form of water creatures among the Ijaw peoples, and the antelope masks of the Ogoni.
Canoe building, including the big canoes used for regattas.
states.attire: Dress varies by people. Kalabari men wear long gowns such as the etibo and the woko, with coral beads, a hat and a walking stick. Women wear layers of wrappers with a blouse, coral beads and a head tie, and Indian madras, called injiri, is a prized cloth. The Ikwerre, Ogoni and other peoples have their own dress.

states.name: Sokoto
states.createdNote: Created on 3 February 1976, when North-Western State was divided into Sokoto and Niger. Kebbi (1991) and Zamfara (1996) were later carved out of it.

population.source: National Population Commission / National Bureau of Statistics projection

states.terrain: Dry, open plains at the edge of the Sahel, with sandy soils and isolated flat-topped hills. The Sokoto and Rima rivers meet near the capital, and their floodplains are the green heart of the state.
states.climate: One of the hottest parts of Nigeria. Afternoon temperatures can pass 45 °C between February and April. Rain falls from about June to October, and the harmattan brings dust and cool nights from late in the year.
states.vegetation: Sahel and Sudan savanna: grassland with thorn trees, baobab and dum palm, and irrigated fields along the rivers.
peoples: Hausa, including the Gobirawa of the old kingdom of Gobir

languages: Arabic, as a language of scholarship and worship

spotlight.title: Nana Asma'u and the women teachers
spotlight.kicker: Scholarship at the heart of the caliphate
spotlight.description: Nana Asma'u (1793–1864) was a daughter of Usman dan Fodio, the scholar whose reform movement founded the Sokoto Caliphate. She wrote poetry and prose in Arabic, Fulfulde and Hausa, advised her brother, the Sultan Muhammad Bello, and is remembered above all as a teacher. She trained a network of women, called jajis, who travelled to villages to teach other women, taking her poems with them as lessons to be learned by heart. Their students were known as the 'yan taru, the associates. The movement still exists, and Nana Asma'u remains a model of women's learning across West Africa.

states.name: Taraba
states.createdNote: Created on 27 August 1991, when Gongola State was divided into Taraba and Adamawa.

population.source: National Population Commission / National Bureau of Statistics projection

states.terrain: The north and west are the broad plains of the Benue and its tributaries, the Taraba and the Donga. The south-east climbs steeply to the Mambilla Plateau, a high grassland at around 1,600 metres, the highest plateau in Nigeria. On its edge, at the Cameroon border, stands Chappal Waddi, the highest point in the country at about 2,419 metres.
states.climate: Hot in the lowlands, with rain from about April to October. The Mambilla Plateau is cool all year, with a much longer wet season.
states.vegetation: Guinea savanna woodland on the plains, with forest along the rivers and in the south; montane grassland and forest on the Mambilla Plateau and in Gashaka-Gumti.
peoples: Kuteb, Chamba, Ichen, Tiv, Wurkun, Jenjo, Yandang and Tigon, among many others

languages: Hausa and Fulfulde, as common languages

spotlight.title: The Aku Uka and the legacy of Kwararafa
spotlight.kicker: Wukari, seat of the Jukun kingship
spotlight.description: The Jukun king, the Aku Uka, holds one of the most ancient offices in central Nigeria. The chronicles of their neighbours remember Kwararafa, a many-peopled power on the Benue whose armies attacked Kano in the 16th and 17th centuries and reached Borno in 1680. The Jukun kings of Wukari became its heirs. The Aku was a sacred king, regarded as the representative of God on earth, and his installation and the festivals of the Jukun year still draw the whole people to the town.

states.name: Yobe
states.createdNote: Carved out of Borno State on 27 August 1991.

population.source: National Population Commission / National Bureau of Statistics projection

states.terrain: Flat, dry plains on the southern edge of the Sahara. The north is sandy, with dunes and scattered oases around Yusufari. The Komadugu Yobe river crosses the north on its way to Lake Chad, and where it is joined by the Hadejia it spreads into wetlands around Nguru and Gashua.

states.vegetation: Sahel savanna in the north, with thorn scrub, grass and dum palms; Sudan savanna in the south.

spotlight.title: The Dufuna canoe
spotlight.kicker: The oldest boat in Africa
spotlight.description: In 1987 a herdsman digging a well near the village of Dufuna struck wood about five metres down. It proved to be a dugout canoe, more than eight metres long and carved from a single trunk with skill that shows a long tradition behind it. Radiocarbon dating put its age at about 8,000 years, which makes it the oldest boat yet found in Africa and one of the oldest in the world. It was made when this dry country was a land of lakes and rivers at the edge of a far larger Lake Chad. The canoe is kept in Damaturu.

states.name: Zamfara
states.createdNote: Carved out of Sokoto State on 1 October 1996.

population.source: National Population Commission / National Bureau of Statistics projection

states.terrain: Broad plains crossed by seasonal rivers that run north and west towards the Sokoto and the Rima. Rocky hills rise in the south and east, among them the great rock of Kwatarkwashi.
states.climate: Hot, with temperatures above 38 °C between March and May. Rain falls from late May to September, and the harmattan blows through the cool dry months.
states.vegetation: Sudan savanna, almost all of it farmed, with woodland in the southern hills.
peoples: Hausa, including the Zamfarawa, Gobirawa and Burmawa
Smaller communities from other parts of Nigeria, mainly in Gusau
languages: Arabic, as a language of scholarship and worship

spotlight.title: Sarkin Noma
spotlight.kicker: Farming is our pride
spotlight.description: The state's slogan says it plainly. In Hausa farming communities a leading farmer can hold the title Sarkin Noma, king of farming. Millet, guinea corn, maize, rice, groundnuts and cotton are the wealth of this country. When the railway reached Gusau in 1927, the town became a major collecting point for cotton and groundnuts. Communal work parties, called gayya, bring neighbours together to work one another's fields.

history.event: The kingdom of Zamfara grows up, with its first capital at Dutsi.
Gobir destroys Birnin Zamfara, the kingdom's capital.
Zamfara becomes part of the Sokoto Caliphate. Its kings later settle at Anka.
The railway reaches Gusau.
Zamfara State is created on 1 October.
Zamfara becomes the first state in Nigeria to extend Sharia to criminal law.
Rural areas have suffered attacks and kidnappings by armed gangs, and many people have been displaced.

didYouKnow: The state's slogan is Farming is Our Pride.
More than four in five people in Zamfara work in farming.
Gold has been mined in the state for many years, mostly by hand.
Zamfara was one of six states created on 1 October 1996.
